source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Causal reasoning in New Caledonian crows: ruling out spatial analogies and sampling error (Commun Integr Biol)
finding: Follow-up to the 2009 Proc B paper. It tests two rival explanations: that crows simply avoid holes, and that they use a spatial rule. Neither fits.
numbers: Sampling test: 8 naive crows learned a stick-tool hole task, then got the trap-table (20 trials each, trap side alternating); none was above chance (all p>.05). Across all 14 crows given the trap-table, only the 3 that had solved the trap-tube passed. Spatial test: 3 passing crows got an inverted two-trap tube; no end preference (all p>.05).
limits: Same lab as the 2009 paper, so not an outside replication. The page text gives no per-crow first-trial counts or exact p values; those sit in figures. This closes the 'abstract only' status of the 14-crow follow-up.
agent_relevance: The control that matters: a naive group with no training on the source task must score at chance on the transfer item. Without it a pass can come from a built-in bias.

source: Tebbich, Seed, Emery, Clayton (2007) Non-tool-using rooks, Corvus frugilegus, solve the trap-tube problem (Animal Cognition 10:225-231)
finding: An outside lab (Cambridge/Vienna) gave a modified trap-tube to rooks. Some solved it. None passed the novel transfer tasks.
numbers: N = 7 rooks. 3 of 7 passed the modified trap-tube. 0 passed the transfer tasks (per the abstract record).
limits: Read from the Europe PMC abstract record only, not the full paper. Task is a modified trap-tube, not the exact 2009 three-transfer series.
agent_relevance: Best outside-lab evidence on the gap: passing the training task is common, passing transfer is rare. Count 'passed training' and 'passed transfer' separately.

source: Bagotskaia, Smirnova, Zorina (2013) Solution of trap tube test by hooded crows (Corvus cornix) (Zh Obshch Biol 74:23-33, Russian, English abstract)
finding: A Moscow lab tested hooded crows on the trap-tube. Most solved by trial and error. Only one solved from the first trial.
numbers: N = 8 crows. Of 6 that learned the piston task, 1 avoided the trap on the first trial and 4 solved it by trial and error. Two transfer tests followed; the authors say behaviour followed concrete rules, not relative position.
limits: Abstract only. Pass counts for the transfer tests are not given in the record. A different species from the New Caledonian crow.
agent_relevance: A first-trial pass is rare even in a related corvid (1 of 6). Score first-trial and learned-in-task separately, as Hennefield 2018 does.

source: Teschke, Tebbich (2011) Physical cognition and tool-use: performance of Darwin's finches in the two-trap tube task (Animal Cognition 14:555-563)
finding: Darwin's finches on the two-trap tube. Few solved it. None transferred when task features changed.
numbers: 0 small tree finches solved it; 2 non-tool-using woodpecker finches solved it; 1 tool-using woodpecker finch solved it with its own tool. 0 transfers.
limits: Abstract record only; N not given there.
agent_relevance: Second outside lab with a no-transfer result. Pattern across rooks, finches and hooded crows: no transfer reported outside the Taylor lab.

source: van Horik, Emery (2016) Transfer of physical understanding in a non-tool-using parrot (Animal Cognition 19:1195-1203)
finding: Trap-gaps paradigm (a cousin of the trap-tube) in macaws and caiques. One bird transferred at first exposure. The group did not.
numbers: N = 8 (4 red-shouldered macaws, 4 black-headed caiques). Initial task: 6 of 8 reached criterion, 4 of 8 correct on trial 1. Transfer task: 5 of 6 correct on trial 1, 4 of 6 reached criterion. Only the caique Red showed clear transfer, 9 of 10 trials correct at first exposure. Group stats: initial task chi2=25.86, df=16, p=.06; transfer chi2=26.67, df=12, p=.009.
limits: Tiny sample. Initial learning criterion was weak. Authors say the Trays-Gaps switch may be a reversal-learning task and birds may have used perceptual cues or side bias.
agent_relevance: Even the best case in an outside lab is 1 bird of 8, with confounds named by the authors. Do not treat one first-trial pass as evidence of a rule.

source: Lambert et al. (2025) No sex differences in learning trap-gap problems in zebra finches (Ecol Evol)
finding: Large-sample trap-gap test with a switch to the other task. Transfer was at chance. Birds used absolute cues (the large gap, the small tray), not a relation.
numbers: 34 birds analysed of 37 bred. Trials to criterion mean 111 (SD 66), median 98, range 23-232; 4 birds never reached criterion. Transfer errors out of 15: mean 7 (SD 2) for both sexes. Tray-first birds 3.6 times as likely to reach criterion (95% CI 1.7-7.8, p=.001).
limits: Trap-gap, not trap-tube. Not a causal-reasoning test by the authors' own account. No first-trial figure given.
agent_relevance: With N=34, transfer is at chance. It shows what cue learning looks like when sample size is large enough to see it.

source: Muller et al. (2016) Inhibitory control, but not prolonged object-related experience, appears to affect physical problem-solving in dogs (PLoS One)
finding: Border collies on four physical tasks including the trap tube. The trap tube was dropped from analysis for floor effects. Dogs treated each task as new.
numbers: 63 recruited, 41 completed the study. 25 dogs ran the trap tube for 50 trials. 'No subject reached 60% correct choices in the last two sessions.' String-pulling did not predict on-off performance (chi2(1)=0.01, p=.93).
limits: Read the first 100,000 characters of the page. Trap tube first-trial data sits in supplementary material not seen.
agent_relevance: A mammal null on the same paradigm: the task is hard to learn at all, so a pass on transfer is rare and should be checked for task-learning first.

source: Logan, Jelbert, Breen, Gray, Taylor (2014) Modifications to the Aesop's Fable paradigm change New Caledonian crow performances (PLoS One 9:e103049)
finding: Eight crows, eight Aesop experiments. Birds pass the simple ones and fail the ones where the cue is removed or the causal rule is less visible. Removing the colour cue broke performance.
numbers: N = 8 crows, 4-6 per experiment, 20 trials each. Water vs sand: 3 passed. Sinking vs floating: all 6. Solid vs hollow: all 6. Wide vs narrow equal water: 4 of 6. Coloured U-tube: 1 passed. Uncovered U-tube (colour cue removed): 0 passed, connected tube chosen 44%. First-trial: experiments 1-3 15/17 correct (p=.002); experiments 4-5 5/10; experiments 6-7 5/10 (p=1.00).
limits: Same lab again (Taylor, Gray). Uncorrected binomial first-trial tests. Hennefield 2018 reanalyses these data and finds a first-trial preference for solid objects.
agent_relevance: The cue-removal analogue in the Aesop line is a failure (0 of the tested birds on the uncovered U-tube). It supports the idea that passes depend on a visible cue.

source: Hennefield, Hwang, Povinelli (2018) Fable or fact: meta-analysis of Aesop's fable studies (Animal Cognition)
finding: Re-analysis of five papers (33 tasks) separates the first-trial preference from learning during the task. Water-vs-sand and float-vs-sink show learning from success and no first-trial preference. Hollow-vs-solid shows a strong first-trial preference for the solid object and no learning.
numbers: N = 28 birds (rooks, jays, NC crows); median 4 per task; 20 trials per bird (15 for jays). First-trial intercept OR: water vs sand 0.53 [0.27,1.07] p=.08; float vs sink 1.23 [0.17,9.18] p=.84; hollow vs solid 57.02 [10.18,319.33] p<.001. Learning slope per insertion OR: water vs sand 1.04 p<.001; float vs sink 1.05 p<.001; hollow vs solid 1.01 p=.67. After a successful water choice OR 5.00 (p<.001); after a failed sand choice OR 0.67 (p=.08). Task order OR 0.81 [0.57,1.14] p=.22 (no transfer between tasks).
quote: did not transfer information learned in one task to subsequent tasks
limits: Very small samples per task. Model assumes a logistic learning curve. Authors still say learning is explained by associative or first-order relational learning.
agent_relevance: This is the number set for gap 7. About 2 of 3 tasks show learning inside the task and no first-trial edge. Score agents the same way: first-trial accuracy and slope are different questions.

source: Ghirlanda, Lind (2017) Aesop's fable experiments demonstrate trial-and-error learning in birds, but no causal understanding (Animal Behaviour 123:239-247)
finding: Re-examines all published Aesop's fable experiments with a method that separates initial performance from learning during the experiment. Concludes there is no evidence yet of causal understanding.
numbers: 23,928 choices by 36 birds of three species (rooks, New Caledonian crows, Eurasian jays). 33 experiments; in 11 of them the group result looked like understanding, but trial-and-error learning could explain each one (per secondary summary).
quote: Aesop's fable experiments have not yet produced evidence of causal understanding
limits: Only the abstract record and a search summary were read. The per-experiment fits are in the paper and in a Figshare data zip, not opened. 36 birds here and 28 in Hennefield reflect different paper sets.
agent_relevance: Same message as Hennefield: before crediting a pass, fit initial performance and learning separately.

source: Mecattaf, Slater, Voudouris, Crosby, Cheke, Shanahan, et al. (2024) A little less conversation, a little more action, please: investigating the physical common-sense of LLMs in a 3D embodied environment
finding: Three multimodal LLMs with ReAct prompting play 40 Animal-AI tasks (4 per level, 10 levels). Children beat the LLMs at every level. An in-context expert example did not help overall.
numbers: Models: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, temperature 0, 3 runs each, so n=12 trials per level. Child baseline stated as 59 children aged 6-10 (Fig 3 caption and appendix). LLMs 'never exceed' the top 10 competition agents; comparable to competition agents at L3, L8, L9, L10 only at very low success. Experiment 2 (in-context example on levels 1-3): no notable overall change; GPT rose at L2 and L3, Gemini fell at L2 and L3, Claude fell at L1.
limits: Per-task results are shown only in a figure of per-level proportions; the paper gives no per-task trap-tube numbers, so gap 4 per-task part stays open. No scaffold-vs-plain comparison. Level 10 'causal reasoning' is coloured surroundings, not a trap-tube. Coarse action space.
agent_relevance: No published plain-vs-scaffold test on Animal-AI trap items. The only prompt variant tried (one in-context example) gave a mixed result, so prompt text alone is not a scaffold test.

source: Voudouris et al. (2022) Direct human-AI comparison in the Animal-AI Environment (Front Psychol 13:711821)
finding: Children vs 30 competition AIs on the same 40 tasks. Children scored far higher. Source of the child baseline.
numbers: Analysis uses N = 52 children and N = 30 AIs (80 df). Children median 0.6276, mean 0.6052, SD 0.1476; AIs median 0.3529, mean 0.3412, SD 0.0809. Agent-type effect F(1,80)=92.381, p<.00001. Outliers by the 1.5xIQR rule: 8 children (44 left), 2 AIs (28 left). 0% of AIs passed levels 3, 6, 8, 9, 10 on average.
limits: I found '52 children' in this paper's analysis text, and 'children (n=59)' in Mecattaf 2024. I did not find a '59' in the Voudouris text I could search. So the 52 versus 59 split is a real discrepancy between the two papers. A reasonable guess is recruited versus analysed, but that is a guess.
agent_relevance: Quote the child baseline as 'about 52 analysed children (Voudouris 2022)' and flag Mecattaf's 59 as a second figure. Do not mix them in one table.

source: Bugaud (2026) CheeseBench: evaluating LLMs on rodent behavioural neuroscience paradigms (ablations)
finding: The 'CoT hurts' result comes from an ablation on one small open-weight model. It does not show that CoT hurts frontier models.
numbers: Ablations used Qwen2.5-VL-7B (32B for the vision ablation), a flat 15 trials per environment, binomial 95% CI about +-25pp. Prompt: default 46.7%, CoT 31.9%, minimal 35.6%, few-shot 29.6%. Authors' reason: step-by-step output 'appears to waste context tokens' that displace useful observation history. Frontier overall (no CoT ablation): Claude Opus 4.7 86.7, GPT-5.2-Codex 82.2, Opus 4.6 82.2, Sonnet 4.6 81.1; rodent reference 78.9.
limits: CoT vs default gap of 14.8pp is inside the stated noise band for a single cell. Authors call trends directional. Context was short (history 5).
agent_relevance: Answers gap 5 in part: CoT cost showed up when output length crowded a small context. Test CoT at equal total tokens, not equal calls.

source: Jin et al. (2023) CLadder, Table 2 and Table 6 (v1.5 and v1.0)
finding: CausalCoT's gain depends on dataset version and on how far the story is from training data. Gain is larger on anti-commonsense stories.
numbers: v1.5: vanilla GPT-4 62.03 overall; by rung 63.01 / 62.82 / 60.55; by alignment commonsense 62.27, nonsense 63.09, anti-commonsense 60.47. CausalCoT 70.40 overall; rungs 83.35 / 67.47 / 62.05; commonsense 69.25, nonsense 71.58, anti-commonsense 70.12. Gain on anti-commonsense +9.65. v1.0: CausalCoT 66.64 vs GPT-4 64.28, only +2.36 overall. Random 49.27.
limits: Rung 3 gain over vanilla is 1.5 points (62.05 vs 60.55). The row order in the PDF table is garbled; rows were matched by position and by the text's own '1.8 points lower' and '9.65 points' statements. GPT-4 is the May 2023 model. No self-consistency or equal-token baseline.
agent_relevance: CoT helped when it was a fixed procedure (graph, query type, formula). Gain at rung 3 was almost nil. Do not read 83 / 67 / 62 as a general 'reasoning helps' result.

source: Samiei et al. (2026) Human adults and LLMs as scientists: who benefits from active exploration? (arXiv 2606.06464)
finding: Current reasoning models (gpt-5, deepseek-reasoner) are near-perfect on the disjunctive rule. The conjunctive condition still has a different, more mixed error profile. LLMs explore less efficiently than top humans.
numbers: Models: gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, gemini-2.5-flash, deepseek-reasoner, o4-mini, deepseek-chat. Humans: average adults ran about 9.6 tests (AND) vs 6.4 (OR); 16% of average adults got both rule and objects wrong on AND and another 16% got the rule right but the objects wrong. gpt-5 spent about 40 s per test on AND (43 s on OR) against about 20 s for humans.
limits: Per-model AND accuracies are in a garbled table and figure; I could not read exact values. Conference paper. No equal-token comparison and no hypothesis-sampling arm.
agent_relevance: The AND gap is smaller for reasoning models but not gone. The hypothesis-sampling fix of GX-Chen 2025 has not been re-tested at equal tokens on these models, so gap 6 second half stays open.

source: Silva, Page, Silva (2005) Methodological-conceptual problems in the study of chimpanzees' folk physics: how studies with adult humans can help (Learning & Behavior 33:47-58)
finding: Adults fail the 'inverted trap' control in the same way apes do, yet they obviously understand traps. So a failure on that control cannot prove a lack of causal knowledge.
numbers: Exp 1: 10 undergraduates, real trap-tubes. Functional traps: 40/40 and 10/10 correct (p<.001). Ineffective traps: tool inserted into the far end on 36 of 40 trials (p<.001). Exp 2 (24 students, schematics): same pattern, 132/144 for group 1 and 54/72 for group 2 (both p<.001). Exp 3 (19 students, trap-table, ineffective hole): 15/19 and 16/19 pulled the rake on the side without the hole (p=.02, p=.005); 15/19 and 16/19 gave the reason that this avoids losing the reward.
limits: Small samples, single trial per person, schematic tasks. The authors argue a first response is the 'gold standard', with no pretraining.
agent_relevance: For gap 8: a fair pass criterion is the high-level pattern across many configurations, not one control. Require correct choices on functional traps and a written reason that cites the causal feature; do not demand perfect behaviour on ineffective-trap items.

source: Shi, Pang, Li (2026) Matched Capabilities, Different Behaviors: a controlled study of MCP and CLI interfaces for language agents (arXiv 2610.34298)
finding: Same operations, same runtime, only the interface format changed. Task performance and cost changed a lot, and so did which actions were chosen and how errors were recovered.
numbers: 6 models, 3 interactive environments. Paired trajectories diverge in a structured way in 94.3% of 2,004 episodes. A repair method (DART) that keeps the semantic choice and fixes only the interface wording raised score in all 6 settings by up to 9.0 points and cut MCP token cost by up to 27.1k tokens per task.
limits: Abstract page only; per-model rates and environment names not read. Tool-use tasks, not causal transfer tasks. Preprint from 25 Oct 2026.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gap 9 that the action format alone moves agent outcomes. A transfer test must hold the interface fixed, or re-run failed items with a simplified interface.

finding: The same model scored between 20% and 57% depending only on interface settings (history length and action batch size).
numbers: History: h=1 57.0%, h=3 about 47%, h=5 about 31%, h=10 26.7%. Action batch size: k=1 28.9%, k=4 51.9%, k=8 45.9%, k=16 20.0%. Qwen2.5-VL-7B, 15 trials per environment. Authors: results 'characterize the agent-plus-interface system, not the model in isolation'.
limits: Small-model, small-sample ablation. Rodent maze tasks, not a causal transfer task.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 in numbers. A harness that sends 16 actions at a time or 10 steps of history can cost 30 points with no change in causal knowledge. Fix and report interface parameters before comparing scaffolds.

source: Europe PMC records, 2026: CausalReasonBench (Research Square preprint PPR1176784) and a clinical Pearl-ladder study (npj Digit Med 42020503)
finding: Two 2026 records bear on CoT and the ladder, but only as abstracts. A prompt that asks Socratic questions beat plain chain-of-thought on counterfactuals. A clinical study found a drop from association to counterfactual queries in most models.
numbers: CausalReasonBench: 384 instances; Socratic prompting beat CoT on counterfactuals by +0.09 CAR; correlation-read-as-causation errors above 40%. Clinical study: 99 scenarios on Pearl's ladder; GPT-o1 AUROC 0.80 vs Llama-3.2-8b 0.73 overall; counterfactual 0.84 vs 0.69.
limits: Abstract-level only, one is a non-peer-reviewed preprint, and neither uses CLadder. Does not close gap 10: no 2025-2026 re-run of CLadder with equal-token baselines was found (search quota and API limits stopped further looking).
agent_relevance: The direction (rung 3 hardest, structured prompts beat free CoT on counterfactuals) matches CLadder, but is weak evidence.
